title: The Royal Albert Hall’s echo took 98 years and a ceiling of giant ‘mushrooms’ to fix

cover.alt: Dozens of large round fibreglass discs hanging below the domed ceiling of the Royal Albert Hall, lit pink and purple above the tiers of boxes.

body: Queen Victoria opened London’s Royal Albert Hall on 29 March 1871, and its acoustic problems became obvious at the very first concert: the huge oval hall under its glass dome threw back a strong echo. Engineers tried more than one cure, but the acoustics were not properly tackled until **1969**, when large fibreglass acoustic diffusing discs, nicknamed ‘mushrooms’ or ‘flying saucers’, were hung below the ceiling to scatter the sound instead of letting it bounce straight back.

slides.heading: Put the echo fixes in order, first to last
items: A canvas awning below the dome
slides.explanation: The awning came first and also kept the sun off the audience. The aluminium panels replaced it in 1949, and the discs went up in 1969.
